title: Historical Background: 2000 Years of the Parallel Postulate
content: Euclid's fifth postulate (the parallel postulate) was suspected for millennia to be provable from the other four axioms. Saccheri (1733) attempted this by assuming it false and deriving contradictions — instead discovering what we now call neutral geometry. Legendre (1794) refined the angle-sum approach: proving the angle sum of any triangle is $\leq \pi$ in neutral geometry. When Bolyai and Lobachevsky (1830s) independently constructed consistent non-Euclidean geometries where angle sum $< \pi$, it became clear the parallel postulate is truly independent. The equivalence 'angle sum $= \pi$ for all triangles $\Leftrightarrow$ parallel postulate' crystallized the distinction between Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry. This file imports `ParallelPostulateIndependence` to use the already-proved independence result in the hyperbolic consequence theorem.
mathContext: Neutral (absolute) geometry: satisfies all Euclid's axioms except the parallel postulate; both Euclidean ($\theta = \pi$) and hyperbolic ($\theta < \pi$) are models

title: GeomTriangle and AngledNeutralGeometry
content: The `GeomTriangle` structure is a minimal representation: three `GeomPoint` fields (from the `ParallelPostulateIndependence` framework), with non-degeneracy as a precondition on theorems rather than a structural requirement. The `AngledNeutralGeometry` extends `NeutralGeometry` (which itself extends `IncidenceGeometry`) with a `triangleAngleSum : GeomTriangle → ℝ` function. This design choice — axiomatizing the angle sum as an abstract real-valued function rather than defining it via `arccos` — separates the logical content (the equivalences and inequalities) from the metric computation, enabling cleaner proofs of the abstract theorems.
mathContext: An angled neutral geometry is $\mathcal{G} = (\text{NeutralGeometry}, \theta)$ where $\theta: \text{Triangle} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies neutral geometry constraints including $\theta(T) \leq \pi$

title: Saccheri-Legendre Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: The Saccheri-Legendre theorem — the angle sum of any triangle in neutral geometry is $\leq \pi$ — is one of the deepest results in absolute geometry. The classical proof uses the Archimedean axiom: given a triangle with angle sum $\pi + \varepsilon$, one constructs a triangle with the same angle sum but arbitrarily small angles (by repeated halving), eventually contradicting the fact that angles are positive. This requires 200-400 lines of betweenness and congruence axioms not yet in Mathlib 4. The axiom `saccheri_legendre : G.triangleAngleSum t ≤ Real.pi` is mathematically justified (it is a theorem) but states it without proof. The `angle_sum_le_pi` theorem is an immediate wrapper.
mathContext: For any triangle $T$ in neutral geometry: $\theta(T) \leq \pi$. Classical proof: if $\theta(T) = \pi + \varepsilon$, halving produces $T'$ with $\theta(T') \geq \pi + \varepsilon/2$, contradicting Archimedean property

title: Defect Transitivity: Zero Defect Propagates
content: The angle defect of a triangle is $d(T) = \pi - \theta(T) \geq 0$ (by Saccheri-Legendre). The defect is additive under triangle decomposition: if $T$ is split into $T_1$ and $T_2$, then $d(T) = d(T_1) + d(T_2)$. This additivity implies: if $d(T_0) = 0$ for some $T_0$, then any triangle can be expressed as a combination of sub-triangles including $T_0$, forcing all defects to zero. In differential geometry, the defect is related to Gaussian curvature via the Gauss-Bonnet theorem: $d(T) = \iint_T K \, dA$ where $K$ is the Gaussian curvature. In Euclidean geometry, $K = 0$; in hyperbolic geometry, $K < 0$.
mathContext: Angle defect $d(T) = \pi - \theta(T)$; additivity: $d(T_1 \cup T_2) = d(T_1) + d(T_2)$; Gauss-Bonnet: $d(T) = -\iint_T K \, dA$ for constant curvature $K$

title: Angle Sum = π ↔ Playfair's Parallel Postulate
content: The axiom `angle_sum_pi_implies_playfair` is the hardest direction: assuming all triangles have angle sum $\pi$, derive Playfair's axiom (through any point not on a line, there is exactly one parallel line). The classical proof constructs a rectangle: four triangles each with angle sum $\pi$ can be assembled into a quadrilateral with four right angles. From a rectangle, Playfair's axiom follows because any line through an interior point must cross both sides, making a unique parallel. This requires Saccheri quadrilateral theory (~500 lines of neutral geometry). The forward direction (`parallel_implies_angle_sum`) is the standard Euclidean proof: alternate interior angles are equal, giving $\theta = \alpha + \beta + \gamma = \pi$.
mathContext: Playfair's axiom: $\forall$ line $\ell$, point $P \notin \ell$, $\exists!$ line through $P$ parallel to $\ell$; equivalent to Euclid's 5th postulate

title: Converse and Full Equivalence
content: The main theorem `angle_sum_implies_parallel` is a one-line application of the axiom `angle_sum_pi_implies_playfair`. The full equivalence `angle_sum_iff_parallel` combines both directions using `⟨angle_sum_implies_parallel G, parallel_implies_angle_sum G⟩` — constructing an `Iff` from its two implications. The proof of the biconditional is notable for its simplicity at the Lean level: once the four axioms are in place, the logical structure is entirely transparent. The mathematical depth is encoded in the axioms, while the Lean proof focuses on combining them correctly.
mathContext: $(\forall T, \theta(T) = \pi) \iff \text{SatisfiesParallelPostulate}(\mathcal{G})$; this is the fundamental dichotomy: Euclidean iff all triangles are 'flat'

title: Hyperbolic Angle Sum < π — The Contradiction Argument
content: The `hyperbolic_angle_sum_lt_pi` theorem proves that any geometry satisfying the hyperbolic parallel property (through any point not on a line, there are at least two distinct parallels) must have angle sum $< \pi$ for every triangle. The proof is a model contradiction argument: (1) Saccheri-Legendre gives $\theta(t) \leq \pi$. (2) If $\theta(t) = \pi$ for any $t$, then defect transitivity gives $\theta = \pi$ for all triangles. (3) Then `angle_sum_implies_parallel` yields Playfair's axiom. (4) But `hyperbolic_contradicts_parallel_postulate` (from `ParallelPostulateIndependence`) says Playfair's axiom and the hyperbolic property are mutually exclusive. The proof uses `by_contra`, `push_neg`, and `le_antisymm` to establish the equality from the negation of strict inequality.
mathContext: Hyperbolic parallel: $\exists$ line $\ell$, point $P$, at least 2 parallels to $\ell$ through $P$. Then $\theta(T) < \pi$ for all $T$: curvature $K < 0$ throughout hyperbolic space

title: Three-File Gallery Arc: Euclidean, Independent, Equivalent
content: The summary section explicitly articulates the three-file proof arc: `TriangleAngleSum.lean` proves angle sum $= \pi$ in the concrete Euclidean model $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a computation); `ParallelPostulateIndependence.lean` proves the parallel postulate is logically independent of the other Euclidean axioms (a model-theoretic construction); and this file proves the abstract equivalence angle sum $= \pi \Leftrightarrow$ Playfair's axiom (a logical synthesis). Together they give a complete formal account of one of geometry's central theorems. This three-part structure — concrete instance, independence, abstract equivalence — is a powerful pattern for formalizing foundational mathematics.
